title: Why Sully.ai Is the Best Dragon Copilot Alternative 2026
summary: Dragon Copilot documents visits at an enterprise price—but stops before claims or scheduling. Sully.ai runs the full workflow at 80–90% less per role.
body_text: Give Dragon Copilot its due first. Formerly DAX Copilot and now Microsoft's merged ambient-plus-dictation product, it is a serious enterprise tool: deeply embedded in the Epic workflow, ambient notes across dozens of specialties, Dragon Medical One dictation, 58 languages, and ICD-10 coding suggestions [1]. On documentation and Epic depth, it competes with anyone. But Dragon Copilot is a documentation assistant for one clinician, priced at the very top of the market. It does not answer the phone, schedule a patient, run intake, or submit a claim. So the real decision for a health system is not "which assistant documents best." It is "do I want to pay an enterprise premium for documentation, or deploy an autonomous workforce for the whole practice ." That is where Sully.ai is the alternative worth a look. Key Takeaway: The leading Dragon Copilot alternative for health systems is Sully.ai, because it runs an autonomous AI workforce, an AI Scribe, AI Coder, AI Receptionist, and AI Triage Nurse, across the whole patient journey rather than a documentation assistant at the point of care. Dragon Copilot (formerly DAX Copilot) has deep Epic integration, strong ambient notes, and dictation, but it does not answer calls, schedule patients, run triage, or submit claims, its coding is ICD-10 suggestions the clinician applies, and it is the most expensive option at roughly 369 to 830 dollars per provider per month plus setup and a 12-month commitment. Sully covers the full workflow on a single integration across Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth, serving 5,000+ providers at 80 to 90 percent less per role than the human equivalent. Where Dragon Copilot documents the visit and suggests codes, Sully's agents do the work: the Scribe writes the note, the Coder submits the clean claim, and the Receptionist books the follow-up. What Dragon Copilot Does and Why Teams Look for an Alternative Dragon Copilot is the enterprise incumbent in ambient documentation, so it is worth being precise about what it does before talking about where it stops. Where Dragon Copilot Is Strong Dragon Copilot is fully embedded in the Epic workflow, including Haiku, and reaches Athenahealth, Meditech, Cerner, and 200+ other systems through the Dragon Medical One infrastructure [1][2]. It captures ambient conversations across dozens of specialties, writes referral letters and after-visit summaries, supports 58 languages, and now suggests ICD-10 codes [2]. It also pairs ambient capture with full dictation in one product, which a pure scribe does not. For a large Epic shop that wants documentation and dictation, it is a serious option. Where Dragon Copilot Falls Short for Health Systems The gaps are not about the note. They are about everything around it, and about the price. Here is how one group practice put it on a call with our team: A 16-provider practice piloting Dragon Copilot, then still branded DAX, told us the sticking point was cost. At roughly 330 dollars a provider each month it ran well above the alternatives, and what they actually wanted was value for the money and notes they could fully customize. For a group that size, paying an enterprise premium for documentation alone did not add up. That lines up with three patterns the research keeps surfacing. It does not run the front desk. Dragon Copilot does not handle scheduling, patient intake, call management, or triage [2]. Those stay with your staff. Its coding is suggestions, not a submitted claim. Dragon Copilot suggests ICD-10 codes for the clinician to review and apply [2]. It does not submit or validate the claim, so the revenue-cycle work still lands on people. It is a premium documentation assistant, not a workforce. Dragon Copilot focuses on documentation and dictation, not the full practice workflow, and it is the most expensive option: roughly 369 to 830 dollars per provider per month, a one-time setup fee, a 12-month minimum, and a 3 to 6 month enterprise deployment [2]. That is a lot to pay for the note alone. How to Evaluate a Dragon Copilot Alternative Because Dragon Copilot matches the field on documentation and Epic depth, the decision should turn on scope, autonomy, and total cost, not on whose note is a shade better. Documentation Assistant or Autonomous Workforce A premium assistant makes one clinician faster. A workforce removes work across the whole practice: the front desk, intake, documentation, coding, claims, and follow-up. That is the fork in the road, and it matters more than any single feature. Coding Suggestions Versus a Submitted Claim ICD-10 suggestions still leave a person to apply them and submit the claim. Autonomous claim submission is a different outcome for the revenue cycle [2]. Ask which one you are actually buying. Total Cost and Time to Value Dragon Copilot is the most expensive option, with a setup fee, a 12-month commitment, and a 3 to 6 month enterprise rollout [2]. Compare that against one platform that covers several roles at 80 to 90 percent below the human equivalent per role, on a single integration. The honest measure is cost per outcome across the practice, not a premium scribe seat. Sully.ai Compared to Dragon Copilot Across the Clinical Workflow Almost every Dragon Copilot comparison argues about note quality, languages, and Epic depth. On those it competes with anyone, so let us concede them and look at the rest of the visit. Documentation and EHR Integration This is a genuine tie. Both produce strong ambient notes , both integrate deeply with Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth , and Dragon Copilot adds dictation on top. There is no honest integration edge to claim here, so we will not pretend there is one. The difference shows up after the note. Front Desk, Scheduling, and Triage Sully's AI Receptionist answers calls, schedules appointments, and handles outreach, and the AI Triage Nurse runs pre-visit intake. Dragon Copilot does none of this [2]. For a practice buried in phone tag and no-shows, this is the difference that actually moves the day. Coding That Submits the Claim Sully's AI Coder reads the finished note, extracts every ICD-10 and CPT code, and submits a clean claim before a denial has a chance to happen. Dragon Copilot suggests ICD-10 codes for the clinician to apply [2]. Suggest versus submit is a real gap in the revenue cycle . Enterprise Premium Versus Workforce Economics Put it together and the contrast is simple. Dragon Copilot is a documentation assistant priced at the top of the market. Sully is a team of agents that share context and hand off cases across the practice on one integration, at 80 to 90 percent below the human equivalent per role [3]. That is a category difference, not a feature difference. Top Dragon Copilot Alternatives for AI Clinical Documentation If you are building a shortlist, here is how the main options stack up. They serve different needs, so the right pick depends on how much of the practice you want to automate. 1. Sully.ai Best for health systems that want an autonomous workforce, not just a documentation assistant. Sully is the only option here that runs a full AI workforce, an AI Scribe, AI Coder, AI Receptionist, and AI Triage Nurse, across the patient journey on one integration across Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth, at 80 to 90 percent lower cost per role. It operates across 5,000+ providers and has delivered 50M+ hours of AI work. Pick Sully when documentation is only the first thing you want to fix. 2. Suki Best for practices that want a strong point-of-care assistant with voice commands and deep EHR integration. 3. Abridge Best for large Epic-centered enterprises that want an enterprise ambient scribe. 4. Heidi Best for individual clinicians who want a polished self-serve scribe with strong template customization. 5. Freed Best for solo clinicians who want the fastest, lowest-cost self-serve scribe. 6. Nabla Best for practices that want a lightweight ambient scribe and for European or GDPR-driven environments. 7. DeepScribe Best for procedural specialties and teams that need heavy note customization. How to Move From Dragon Copilot to an AI Workforce Moving off Dragon Copilot does not mean giving up the ambient note and dictation clinicians like. It means adding the work that runs on people around it, for less. Mapping the Work Dragon Copilot Leaves to Staff List what still runs on your team around Dragon Copilot: the front desk, scheduling, intake, applying the codes, submitting the claims, and follow-up. That list is exactly the work a workforce absorbs, and the cost the premium price hides. Keeping the Documentation Experience Clinicians Like Clinicians who like the ambient note and dictation lose nothing. Sully's AI Scribe captures documentation during and after the visit and adapts to how each clinician writes. Measuring Front Office and Revenue Cycle Gains Decide the numbers up front: calls answered and appointments booked without staff, claims submitted clean, denial rate, documentation time saved, and total cost per provider against the Dragon Copilot contract. Dragon Copilot cannot move the first two. Choosing the Right AI Workforce for Your Health System The choice was never really which assistant documents best. It is whether you want an enterprise-priced documentation assistant or an autonomous workforce for the practice. Sully.ai is the Dragon Copilot alternative for organizations that want the front desk, triage, documentation, coding, and claims to run as one workforce on one integration, for less. If that is the direction you are headed, the fastest way to see it is to watch the agents hand off on your own EHR. Book a demo and bring your hardest workflow. FAQ Q: What is the best Dragon Copilot alternative for a health system? Sully.ai is the strongest Dragon Copilot alternative for health systems because it runs an autonomous AI workforce, an AI Scribe, AI Coder, AI Receptionist, and AI Triage Nurse, across the whole patient journey on a single integration across Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth, at 80 to 90 percent lower cost per role. Dragon Copilot is a strong documentation assistant, but it does not run the front desk, triage, or claim submission. Q: How much does Dragon Copilot (DAX Copilot) cost? Dragon Copilot uses enterprise pricing without transparent public rates, roughly 369 to 830 dollars per provider per month depending on contract volume, plus a one-time setup fee and a typical 12-month minimum commitment, with enterprise deployment taking 3 to 6 months [2]. Sully.ai prices each AI role 80 to 90 percent below the human equivalent and covers the whole workflow, not just documentation. Q: Does Dragon Copilot handle scheduling, patient calls, or claims? No. Dragon Copilot focuses on ambient documentation, dictation, and ICD-10 coding suggestions. It does not handle front desk, scheduling, patient intake, call management, triage, or autonomous claim submission [2]. Sully.ai's AI Receptionist, AI Triage Nurse, and AI Coder cover those. Q: Is Dragon Copilot the same as DAX Copilot? Yes. DAX, short for Dragon Ambient eXperience, Copilot was rebranded and merged with Dragon Medical One dictation under the Dragon Copilot name by Microsoft in 2025. The ambient documentation core is the same product line. Q: Why would a health system switch from Dragon Copilot to Sully.ai? Because Dragon Copilot documents the visit at an enterprise price, while Sully.ai automates the whole practice, front desk, triage, documentation, coding, and claims, as one connected workforce on a single integration, at 80 to 90 percent below the human equivalent per role. title: Credit Acceptance Announces Leadership Changes to Advance Digital-First Strategy
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Credit Acceptance Corporation's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Print Press Releases << Back Jul 27, 2026 Credit Acceptance Announces Leadership Changes to Advance Digital-First Strategy PDF Version Southfield, Michigan, July 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Credit Acceptance Corporation (Nasdaq: CACC) (referred to as the “Company”, “Credit Acceptance”, “we”, “our”, or “us”), announced leadership changes designed to advance our digital-first strategy and position the Company for long-term success. Siddharth Lal is joining the Company as Chief Marketing Officer. In this role, Mr. Lal will lead Credit Acceptance’s Marketing organization and will have ongoing executive leadership responsibility for Product, bringing the Company’s customer, dealer, product, and brand efforts under a more integrated leadership structure. He will lead efforts to deepen customer insights, enhance dealer and consumer engagement; bring innovative products and solutions to market; and support the Company’s next phase of growth and evolution. Mr. Lal has significant experience leading growth at scale and a strong understanding of customer needs across a wide range of consumer segments, including subprime consumers. During more than 20 years at T-Mobile, most recently as Senior Vice President – Commercial Management, he helped drive customer growth, sharpen the company’s market position, and build high-performing teams with strong commercial execution. “Under Sid’s leadership, we will deepen our understanding of our customers, build differentiated products, and deliver experiences that are simpler, faster, and more effective,” said Vinayak Hegde, Chief Executive Officer. “Sid brings deep expertise in Product, Marketing, and business transformation, along with a proven ability to translate strategy into growth.” “I am excited to partner with an exceptional leadership team, to serve my team and the organization, and to work alongside an incredible network of dealers,” said Mr. Lal. “The focus is clear: drive growth and retention with the consumer, the dealer, and the team at the center, through a digital-first strategy that simplifies and improves the experience for all, creating real and lasting value.” The Company also has hired and plans to announce a new Chief Technology Officer in late August. These executive leadership changes reflect the Company’s decision to bring leaders with proven transformation experience and new capabilities to product, marketing, and technology as we advance the next phase of our digital-first strategy. Mr. Hegde will work closely with the leadership team to maintain momentum across the Company’s product roadmap, technology modernization efforts, and dealer and consumer experience initiatives. In connection with these changes, Andrew Rostami, Chief Product and Marketing Officer, and Ravi Mohan, Chief Technology Officer, will step down, effective August 14, 2026. The Company expects both leaders to support a smooth transition of responsibilities in the next six months and appreciates their contributions during a period of modernization and change. “Andrew and Ravi have made important contributions to Credit Acceptance during a period of modernization and change,” said Mr. Hegde. “Andrew helped strengthen our Product and Marketing capabilities and advanced important growth initiatives, while Ravi helped modernize our technology foundation and accelerate the delivery of digital capabilities. We are grateful for their leadership and appreciate their continued support to help ensure a smooth transition.” Finally, Kenneth Booth announced his retirement from the Company’s board of directors (the “Board”) on July 21, 2026. In November 2025, Mr. Booth had agreed to remain on the Company’s Board to support Mr. Hegde’s transition to Chief Executive Officer following his long career with Credit Acceptance, which included serving as the Chief Executive Officer and President. The Board has reduced its size from six to five directors with no immediate plans to add another director. “After a more than 20-year career with Credit Acceptance, I remained on the Board to support Vinayak and the executive team and helped ensure the Company was well positioned for continued success. With that transition now complete, I believe this is the right time for me to retire from the Board,” Mr. Booth said. “While I am stepping away from my formal role, I will continue to be a proud shareholder and supporter of the Company." “Ken's leadership and stewardship have had a profound impact on Credit Acceptance. He helped build a strong and enduring Company while remaining deeply committed to our mission and values. We are grateful for his many contributions and for the support he provided,” Mr. Hegde said. “On behalf of everyone at Credit Acceptance, I thank Ken for his service and wish him the very best in retirement.” Together, these changes are designed to support continuity in execution and align the Company’s leadership structure with our next phase of growth. Description of Credit Acceptance Corporation We make vehicle ownership possible by providing innovative financing solutions that enable automobile dealers to sell vehicles to consumers regardless of their credit history. Our financing programs are offered through a nationwide network of automobile dealers who benefit from sales of vehicles to consumers who otherwise could not obtain financing; from repeat and referral sales generated by these same customers; and from sales to customers responding to advertisements for our financing programs, but who actually end up qualifying for traditional financing. Without our financing programs, consumers are often unable to purchase vehicles or they purchase unreliable ones. Further, as we report to the three national credit reporting agencies, an important ancillary benefit of our programs is that we provide consumers with an opportunity to improve their lives by improving their credit score and move on to more traditional sources of financing. Credit Acceptance is publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the symbol CACC. For more information, visit creditacceptance.com. title: The Deadliest Decade: The Most Lethal Racing Incident You’ve Never Heard Of
summary: Yellow River Drag Strip was an outlaw track. Not an outlaw in the sense that it was illegal or a lone pariah that operated beyond the norms of polite society. On the contrary. Yellow River was one of a legion of scruffy drag strips that dotted backwaters all over the country, from the overgrown pastures […]
body_text: Yellow River Drag Strip was an outlaw track. Not an outlaw in the sense that it was illegal or a lone pariah that operated beyond the norms of polite society. On the contrary. Yellow River was one of a legion of scruffy drag strips that dotted backwaters all over the country, from the overgrown pastures of the rural South to the featureless sprawl of the exurban West. “A lot of them were back in the woods, and you needed a map just to find them,” said Don Prudhomme, who visited just about all of them during his long career. What made these tracks outlaws was the fact that they weren’t sanctioned by the National Hot Rod Association or the American Hot Rod Association. Instead of big-time events featuring full fields of national stars, they catered mostly to local run-what-you-brung competition—a motley mixture of fair-weather drag racers in street-legal cars and semi-pro ringers with more moxie than money. Dick Brannan in the Bob Ford 427 SOHC Mustang was a leading factory-backed figure at the time, representing Ford Motor Company’s drag racing program in mid-’60s sanctioned Funny Car competitions. ISC Archives/CQ-Roll Call Group/Getty Images [The Deadliest Decade chronicles pro racing from 1964 to 1973, when the influx of money and technology caused speeds to skyrocket while racetracks remained unchanged. The carnage that followed sparked outrage that transformed attitudes about safety and spawned the creation of the modern safety industry. This is the second of three excerpts, and you can read the first here . The book is available for preorder at Octane Press . — Ed. ] For outlaw tracks, the money shows were “booked in” slates of match races hyped through newspaper ads, flyers, and radio spots exhorting listeners to “BEEE THERRRRRE!!!” NHRA and AHRA races featured a series of elimination rounds until the two last remaining cars faced off in the final. A typical match race, on the other hand, involved two headliners who were usually paid a flat fee to race heads-up in a best two-out-of-three format. On special occasions, to boost attendance, promoters would put together a “Chicago-style” show with four racers competing on a round-robin basis. And that’s exactly what drew 5000 fans to Yellow River Drag Strip in Covington, Georgia, on Sunday, March 2, 1969. The Onenota Star The attraction was a quartet of Funny Cars featuring blown, big-block, nitro-gulping engines in tube-frame chassis covered by fiberglass, flip-top bodies that resembled muscle cars of the era. Good ones blasted through the quarter-mile in 8 seconds while going out the back door at more than 180 miles per hour. They weren’t quite as fast as Top Fuel slingshots, but they were more squirrelly going down the track—and more popular with the fans. This made them naturals for the match-race circuit, where spectators were eager to root for their Mopar, Ford, and GM faves. The three out-of-town invitees at Yellow River were Arnie Beswick in the Tameless Tiger Pontiac GTO, Malcolm Durham in the Strip Blazer Corvair, and Frank Oglesby in a Cougar owned by “Dyno Don” Nicholson, who’d recently switched to Pro Stock after deciding that Funny Cars were too hairy for his taste. The local stud was Georgian Huston Platt, who campaigned his Camaro as the Dixie Twister. The chassis came from the Logghe Stamping Company, a top Funny Car builder of the day. Although Chrysler Hemis were the engines of choice in this period, Platt’s mill was a Chevy V-8 bored and stroked to 498 cubic inches and topped by a GMC 6-71 supercharger. The Yellow River property, circa 2026. Google The drag strip consisted of a narrow, two-lane furrow of asphalt cut through a woody Georgia hollow that now houses a mobile home tract about 35 miles east of Atlanta. Although there were chain-link fences and guardrails near the start line, nothing separated the spectators from the rest of the track other than shallow dirt berms. The shutdown area was particularly iffy, with a curve right in the middle. The conditions weren’t ideal, to put it mildly, but they also weren’t especially dubious by the standards of the day, which were, admittedly, not very high. As Platt said later, “There wasn’t a track in 10 states that was qualified to run those cars back then.” By mid-afternoon, the crowd was liquored-up and rowdy. Several PA announcements requesting that spectators move away from the track were ignored. At 2:20 p.m., Platt staged in the right lane for his run against Oglesby. In front of him, the drag strip was flanked by two unbroken lines of people stretching to the finish lights. Platt launched cleanly. But about 1000 feet into the run, he heard a loud bang. He immediately popped his parachute. Although there is a brief clip of amateur video of the wreck, it’s too blurry to show exactly what happened. According to drag racing lore, a foolhardy fan moved toward the track to grab a beer can and was swallowed up by the billowing chute. For whatever reason, the Dixie Twister angled to the right and arced over the dirt berm like a crowd-surfing rock star and thudded into a tightly packed mass of humanity. Contemporary reports say the car was going 150 mph when it hit. Unknown In and of itself, the crash wasn’t serious. If there had been a decent barrier in place, Platt would have walked away unscathed—which, in fact, he did. But because there was no spectator protection, the results were cataclysmic. Eleven spectators died at the scene, and a twelfth died later in the hospital. The youngest was 3 years old, the oldest 65. The rest were in their teens and 20s. More than 40 people were injured. This was the worst tragedy in the history of American motorsports. Yet behind this simple, declarative sentence is a long, complicated story. Although there was plenty of regional coverage of the accident, the Yellow River catastrophe wasn’t a big story in the rest of the country. Today, amazingly, it’s almost completely forgotten. Even drag racers who were active at the time have only a hazy recollection that something really ugly occurred on a really sketchy drag strip somewhere far, far away. This is a comment less on the fallibility of memory than the barbaric safety record of drag racing in the 1960s. Sure, 12 dead and 40-plus injured in a single incident are appalling numbers. But this was an era when the drivers of Top Fuel rails and Funny Cars were killed as regularly as Social Security checks were cut. To understand why carnage was so commonplace requires looking back at the roots of the sport. *** The post The Deadliest Decade: The Most Lethal Racing Incident You’ve Never Heard Of appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: How Clorox is using TikTok Shop to learn, innovate and grow
summary: Learn how Clorox is using TikTok Shop as a learning lab to test products, gain consumer insights and fuel innovation through social commerce.
body_text: Consumers today don’t always discover products the way they did a decade ago. Increasingly, inspiration, entertainment and shopping are all happening in the same place—and for Clorox, that presents an opportunity to learn, connect and innovate in new ways. In a recent Modern Retail feature, Rita Gorenberg, senior director of brand experience, shared how Clorox is using TikTok Shop to explore content, commerce and consumer learning. Highlights from Rita’s perspective How is Clorox approaching TikTok Shop differently? Clorox is treating TikTok Shop as more than a sales channel. The platform serves as a learning lab where brands can test products, gather real-time consumer insights and better understand how consumers engage with content, creators and commerce. What role is social-first content playing? One example is Pine-Sol’s “OMG da Pine” campaign, where the brand has built an engaged following through original characters and creator-inspired content before launching a limited-edition scent collection that sold out within hours. Another is Clorox Pure , which sold out within 10 days of launching on TikTok Shop after the company used creator content to educate consumers about the new allergen-neutralizing category. These efforts demonstrate how social insights can help inform both marketing and innovation strategies. What does this mean for Clorox’s future growth? Clorox is using social commerce to accelerate learning and innovation. Our brands’ early success on TikTok Shop demonstrate how expanding our social commerce helps Clorox identify consumer trends, refine products and create more relevant brand experiences. title: Zoom Revenue Accelerator unveils AI that drives revenue action, not just insights
summary: Read more about: Zoom Revenue Accelerator unveils AI that drives revenue action, not just insights
body_text: New AI capabilities and flexible plans give revenue teams the guidance and coaching they need to sharpen performance and close deals faster. SAN JOSE, Calif., July 22, 2026 — Sales organizations are managing an overwhelming amount of data that too often lives across multiple disconnected systems. When customer interactions, business knowledge, and CRM data are siloed, sellers lose critical context due to systems sprawl, putting them at a disadvantage when advancing sales opportunities. Today, Zoom Communications, Inc. (NASDAQ: ZM) announced updates to Zoom Revenue Accelerator (ZRA), including the general availability of Sales Assist (real-time deal guidance), Ask ZRA (natural language AI inquiries on conversation data), and Sales Roleplay (AI-powered practice simulations), through new Zoom Revenue Accelerator Essentials and Premium offerings. Together, these innovations deliver AI-powered guidance before, during, and after every customer engagement, so that revenue teams can supercharge how they process the information and turn it into real action. These ZRA updates are coming as the need for connected revenue intelligence demand has increased. According to a report from IDC , 34% of sales executives rank improving interoperability between disparate systems as the top driver of their sales initiatives, while 28% say reducing the number of systems and vendors they manage is their highest priority. The findings reflect a shift toward unified platforms that help revenue teams spend less time managing technology and more time driving customer outcomes. What’s New Zoom Revenue Accelerator is expanding with the general availability of Sales Assist, Ask ZRA, and Sales Roleplay, all new AI capabilities that build on its existing conversation intelligence, coaching, and forecasting capabilities. These will be available through new Zoom Revenue Accelerator Essentials and Premium offerings, giving organizations greater flexibility in adopting and scaling advanced AI across their revenue teams. From revenue intelligence to revenue action Zoom Revenue Accelerator helps organizations capture customer conversations, uncover deal insights, strengthen coaching, and improve forecasting. This launch builds on that foundation by helping revenue teams put those insights to work. With Sales Assist, Ask ZRA, and Sales Roleplay, Zoom Revenue Accelerator extends beyond surfacing intelligence to delivering guidance where work happens. This helps sellers prepare for conversations, managers coach more effectively, and organizations continuously improve performance across the revenue lifecycle. The result is a more connected revenue organization where every customer interaction contributes to stronger relationships, healthier pipelines, and more predictable growth. “ Every customer conversation is more than a record of what happened; it’s an opportunity to shape what happens next, ” said Madison Muchow, general manager of Zoom Revenue Accelerator at Zoom . “ We believe AI should do more than summarize interactions; it should help revenue teams prepare smarter by coaching continuously, and execute with confidence to drive more pipeline. That’s the future we’re building at Zoom .” AI that works across the sales workflow From preparation to follow-up, every stage of the sales process offers opportunities to improve execution. Zoom Revenue Accelerator brings together AI, coaching, and revenue intelligence to help teams make the most of every customer interaction. Before the meeting, Sales Roleplay helps organizations strengthen seller performance through AI-powered practice sessions based on realistic customer scenarios, giving sellers personalized guidance that reinforces best practices before the next customer interaction. During live customer conversations, Sales Assist surfaces competitive intelligence, objection guidance, discovery prompts, battlecards, and configurable framework capture in real time, helping sellers stay focused on customers while AI works in the background. After a customer conversation, Ask ZRA enables sellers and managers to ask natural-language questions across customer conversations and revenue data to uncover account history, identify deal risks, understand coaching opportunities, and access the information they need to make the next engagement even better. And because customer intelligence shouldn’t be confined to a single application, MCP Server , including Zoom’s plug-in with OpenAI Codex , securely extends Zoom Revenue Accelerator to compatible AI platforms and enterprise workflows, enabling organizations to bring trusted revenue intelligence wherever work happens. These new capabilities will be available as part of the new Zoom Revenue Accelerator Essentials and Premium offerings. Giving customers more flexibility to adopt AI Organizations are at different stages of their AI journey. To give customers more flexibility in adopting advanced AI capabilities, Zoom is introducing two new offerings: Zoom Revenue Accelerator Essentials coming in August, is designed for organizations looking to strengthen conversation intelligence and sales coaching as they begin their AI journey. It includes foundational Zoom Revenue Accelerator capabilities, along with access to the new Ask ZRA, Sales Assist, and Sales Roleplay features, through a consumption model that lets teams explore advanced AI without overcommitting. Zoom Revenue Accelerator Premium is designed for organizations ready to scale AI across their revenue teams. It includes everything in the Essentials offering, plus unlimited Sales Assist usage, recurring monthly AI credits for Ask ZRA and Sales Roleplay, and enhanced administrative controls that help organizations manage AI adoption across teams. Both offerings reflect Zoom’s new consumption-based approach for advanced AI capabilities, allowing organizations to align costs with adoption while maintaining governance and predictable usage. Find out more about these new offerings at Zoom.com . Zoom Revenue Accelerator Essentials , coming in August, starts at $66 per user per month, billed annually, and Zoom Revenue Accelerator Premium starts at $99.99 per user per month, billed annually. Additional information about packaging and availability is available at Zoom.com . About Zoom Zoom (NASDAQ:ZM) is a system of action for modern work, turning live collaboration into completed results. From entrepreneurs to global enterprises, customers choose Zoom to seamlessly collaborate, communicate, and drive outcomes across meetings, phone, contact center, and more — all with the built-in assistance of Zoom AI. Founded in 2011, Zoom is headquartered in San Jose, CA. For more information, visit zoom.com . Zoom Public Relations Travis Isaman [email protected]
